documents.title: Honor Code (includes Generative AI rule)
documents.stance_why: The Honor Code says AI 'should not be used in the completion of any course assignments, exams, or written work... unless an instructor... has specifically and explicitly authorized their use'. AI is banned unless permitted, so restrict rather than delegates, because a default ban is set.
documents.summary: The student-run Honor Code sets a default ban on generative AI in coursework unless the instructor explicitly authorizes it for an assignment. Passing off AI work as one's own, not citing it, and using it on closed-book exams are Honor Code violations.

units.why: The sentence sets the default ban: AI 'should not be used in the completion of any course assignments, exams, or written work'. It is a default stance (P01), not a fallback rule for silent syllabi, because it names all coursework; the authorization exception is coded separately.
units.anchor: should not be used in the completion of any course assignments, exams, or written work

units.why: The exception 'unless an instructor for a given course has specifically and explicitly authorized their use for the assignment in question' puts the permission decision with the instructor, per assignment. P04 fits better than P06 because the point is who decides, not what applies in silence.
units.anchor: has specifically and explicitly authorized their use for the assignment in question

units.why: Says 'Presenting AI-generated content as original student work' is a violation of the Honor Code. The core rule is that students may not pass off AI output as their own (P19); the misconduct label is secondary, so P36 was not chosen.
units.anchor: Presenting AI-generated content as original student work
units.policy: Presenting AI-generated content as original student work constitutes a violation of the Honor Code.

units.why: Says 'submitting AI-generated content without citing its source in artificial intelligence tools' violates the Honor Code, so citing AI use is required and nondisclosure is a violation. P24 (disclose with each submission) fits; P28 would apply only if the focus were how disclosure is treated in grading.
units.anchor: submitting AI-generated content without citing its source in artificial intelligence tools
units.policy: Submitting AI-generated content without citing its source in artificial intelligence tools constitutes a violation of the Honor Code.

units.why: Says 'relying on generative AI tools for closed-book quizzes, tests, and exams' is a violation. It addresses AI in assessments, so P22 fits.
units.anchor: relying on generative AI tools for closed-book quizzes, tests, and exams
units.policy: Relying on generative AI tools for closed-book quizzes, tests, and exams constitutes a violation of the Honor Code.

documents.title: Generative AI: Privacy and security guidelines (Ask Athena)
documents.stance_why: The page sets no rule on whether AI may be used for coursework; it gives privacy, security and critical-evaluation guidance ('Use College-provided AI tools', 'Always critically evaluate any generative AI output') and points students to the Honor Code. It sets no use stance itself.
documents.summary: LITS guidance on generative AI covering approved College tools, data handling, hallucination and bias, copyright and environmental concerns. It sets no academic-use stance and points students to the Honor Code.

units.why: The opening line states the page's purpose: 'guidelines that support the responsible and ethical use of AI technology, while managing risk'. That is an institution-level framework statement (P56).
units.anchor: guidelines that support the responsible and ethical use of AI technology

units.why: 'Use College-provided AI tools' is a directive to prefer sanctioned tools, justified by data protections. P50 (prefer vetted tools) fits better than P17 because the point is data protection, not provision of a course tool.
units.anchor: Use College-provided AI tools (Firefly, BoodleBox, Microsoft Copilot, Zoom AI Companion)
units.frag_end: answer AI queries made by others.

units.why: States as fact that the tools' terms of service ensure inputs 'will not be used to train AI models'. It explains why vetted tools are preferred, so it is a privacy fact (P50) with modality informs.
units.anchor: will not be used
units.frag_end: answer AI queries made by others.
units.policy: The terms of service of the College-provided AI tools ensure that files, data and text you input and any content you generate will not be used to train AI models or answer AI queries made by others.

units.why: Warns that 'Other tools -- especially free ones -- may lack these protections' and says to review terms. This is a data-protection instruction to check tool terms (P50).
units.anchor: Always review a tool's terms of service and privacy policies carefully

units.why: 'if you must use free tools, avoid uploading private or sensitive information' is a data-protection limit on what goes into AI tools. P50 fits; P20 and P49 concern assignment materials, which is not the point here.
units.anchor: avoid uploading private or sensitive information
units.frag_start: if you must use free tools

units.why: 'Follow all relevant College policies' (Acceptable Use, Data Handling) ties AI use to existing institutional rules. This is a framework cross-reference (P56).
units.anchor: Follow all relevant College policies

units.why: 'Students must also adhere to their Honor Code' links AI use to academic-integrity rules. No type states this cross-reference exactly; P56 (framework) was chosen over P36 because no misconduct classification is stated here.
units.anchor: Students must also adhere to their

units.why: 'Always critically evaluate any generative AI output' tells users to check AI output, matching P31.
units.anchor: Always critically evaluate any generative AI output.

units.why: Explains that tools 'can predict things that are statistically plausible but inaccurate' and may invent citations. It is the stated reason outputs must be verified (P31), given as fact.
units.anchor: can predict things that are statistically plausible but inaccurate or without factual basis
units.frag_end: books and authors that do not exist!

units.why: States that tools 'are vulnerable to biases in their training data'. This names bias as a concern about AI (P53), given as fact.
units.anchor: vulnerable to biases
units.frag_end: books and authors that do not exist!

units.why: 'Look for settings that can help you critically evaluate a bot's output' recommends using tool features such as Copilot's Think Deeper or BoodleBox's Coach mode. P31 fits (verification).
units.anchor: Look for settings that can help you critically evaluate a bot's output

units.why: Says 'applicability of copyright law, moral rights, and fair use to these tools is still under discussion'. A statement about copyright of AI use, so P52.
units.anchor: applicability of copyright law,
units.policy: The applicability of copyright law, moral rights, and fair use to these tools is still under discussion.

units.why: Notes that Adobe Firefly 'prohibit[s] users from uploading copyrighted materials without permission'. This is a tool-terms fact about copyright, so P52 rather than P49 (which binds students' uploads of course materials).
units.anchor: prohibit users from uploading copyrighted materials without permission of the copyright holder

units.why: 'AI processing is energy-intensive' and growth may offset efficiency gains: an environmental concern (P53).
units.anchor: AI processing is energy-intensive

units.why: Cautions that many stories about AI impact come from companies that 'stand to gain from AI's expansion' and urges readers to 'think critically'. It is advice about evaluating sources, closest to P31 (critical evaluation); P53 does not fit since it names no harm.
units.anchor: be sure to think critically about who authored and published this information
units.frag_end: what they stand to gain from it.

units.why: Lists the four College-provided tools with descriptions (BoodleBox with 'privacy and teaching features', Copilot, Firefly, Zoom AI Companion). It says the College provides sanctioned AI tools, so P17.
units.anchor: A collaborative AI workspace with access to many LLM models and privacy and teaching features

notes: No CS department-level AI policy found (CS site only has course pages; CS 109 syllabus is a course document, deferred). Honor Code is the key policy document. Coded by CODER B. Honor Code coded only for the generative-AI paragraph; the rest (procedures, social resolutions) has no AI content.
